articles.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. articles.title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
articles.description: The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so . Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine. The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. That is a meaningful opening, especially since New START expired in February. However, the joint d

articles.title: A gross misreading of 'Yalta' undergirds lame critique of trilateral
articles.description: Representatives of the transatlantic establishment were quick to liken the trilateral summit in Shenzhen to the supposed Anglo-American “ betrayal ” of Poland and other Eastern European states at Yalta in February 1945. Yalta ratified — but did not create — the division of Europe into spheres of influence that later became frozen into the dividing lines of the Cold War. A less apoplectic strain of the same underlying sentiment holds that President Trump’s willingness to meet his Russian and Chinese counterparts is in itself an unnecessary concession to Russia and China that merely signals weakness and does nothing to advance U.S. interests; as if the avoidance of nuclear war with China were not a vital U.S. interest. The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands . Rufo, Susan Crabtree, and Kenneth Schrupp via City Journal , Paradise, California was a quiet town in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Seniors flocked there seeking affordable homes. Others came for abundant land and small-town charm. For more than a century, Paradise was an oasis from the hustle of urban California. On November 8, 2018, it all came crashing down. A hook, suspended from a tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric, one of America's largest utilities, snapped. A jumper conductor hit the tower, melting metal strands and setting nearby vegetation ablaze. Paradise and its surroundings were destroyed: 150,000 acres were incinerated, thousands of homes were leveled, and 85 people were killed. The town's population shrunk by more than half in the five years that followed the infamous Camp Fire. PG&E eventually pleaded guilty to 84 counts of manslaughter. articles.title: Taiwan Strangles The Shorts After The Taiex Loses 5,000 Points In Three Days
articles.description: Taiwan Strangles The Shorts After The Taiex Loses 5,000 Points In Three Days Regulators don't cut a short-selling quota twice in two weeks because the first cut worked. On Thursday, hours after the Taiex plunged 1,768 points or 4.4% to 38,426.89, and the small-cap TPEx crashed 7.2% with more than 280 OTC names locked limit-down, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission tightened the screws again: the intraday cap on short sales of borrowed shares drops from 3% to just 1% of a stock's 30-day average daily volume , and any stock that falls 3.5% or more in a session (down from 10%, i.e. limit-down) can't be shorted below the prior close the next day. The new rules take effect Friday, November 20, according to Goldman's securities lending desk and the FSC's own notice, in what Goldman's Peter Slater calls the second "Short Sell Ban" in as many weeks. As of Thursday's close, that trigger alone covers more than a thousand listed and OTC names, local press reported. This is the second clampdown this month. articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
articles.description: Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls • How to make your phone last longer • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be. While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. articles.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
articles.description: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service No one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? Continue reading...

Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure. Continue reading...

articles.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
articles.description: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. But let’s look on the positive side, suggests Adam Grant, the Wharton organisational psychologist and New York Times bestselling author of Originals, and Hidden Potential. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records
articles.description: Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years. Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added. Continue reading...

articles.title: Dashing through the snow: 10 of the UK’s best Christmas train rides
articles.description: Heritage railways will soon be steaming into action, with special departures offering winter landscapes, seasonal goodies and a chance to meet Father Christmas Red tablecloths, festive decor and tartan upholstered carriage seats bring the yuletide vibe onboard Strathspey Railway’s Elf Express. From your first-class carriage of either a steam-hauled or heritage diesel engine, you will be served sandwiches and cakes from traditional tiered plates, washed down with hot drinks and fizz. Santa and his elves will visit your carriage with presents for children, otherwise sit back and enjoy the woodland and moorland scenery of rural Speyside on this 20-mile round-trip (lasting about 1 hour and 40 minutes) between Aviemore and Broomhill. Weekends and select weekdays until 24 December, £260 for four people . Continue reading...

articles.title: UK businesses: what are the barriers stopping you hiring young people?
articles.description: We want to hear from people who own or run companies in Britain who are trying to hire under-25s. What obstacles do you face? Labour’s long-awaited review into youth joblessness published this week recommended that ministers cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people. Alan Milburn’s report into how to address the nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training in the UK also proposes setting up a youth opportunity service to provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK energy bills are rising. Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal?
articles.description: We’d like to hear from UK households about whether they’re switching energy suppliers to save money or finding that deals are too similar to make it worthwhile Energy bills in Great Britain are forecast to rise by 26% from January, adding £443 to the typical household’s annual bill. The increase, driven by rising gas prices amid the Middle East conflict, would be one of the biggest quarterly rises on record, according to forecaster Cornwall Insight. Are you shopping around for a better gas or electricity deal or have you decided to stay with your current supplier? What has influenced your decision? Continue reading...

articles.title: Bloomscrolling: the uplifting new way to waste your own time
articles.description: Tired of your social media feeds being a bin fire? Want more beauty? Gen Z are training their algorithms – and it’s working wonders for them Name: Bloomscrolling. articles.title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
articles.description: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller • This review contains spoilers Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes . It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.description: Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear. I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her. Continue reading...

articles.title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love
articles.description: Save money and help the planet with these genuine discounts on everything from bamboo toilet paper to B Corp-certified bedding • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops • The best early Black Friday deals Ethical and sustainable probably aren’t the first words that spring to mind when you think of Black Friday. The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. Many of our Filter recommendations tick either the green box or the affordable box, but we (and you, I expect) would be a lot happier if more of them ticked both. Continue reading...

articles.title: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist
articles.description: Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems . Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album?
articles.description: (Warp) The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the i

articles.title: You be the judge: should my friend stop eating smelly meals at work?
articles.description: Mina’s substantial, aromatic workplace breakfasts and lunches are a concern for her friend and colleague Jackie. You decide who’s making a meal of the situation • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror I recommended Mina as an intern but now worry as she’s always eating pungent food at her desk Who says you can only eat simple meals in the office? It’s fun to be creative with food Continue reading...

articles.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
articles.description: UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home. A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera . Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The abuse I copped was phenomenal’: researchers accuse tobacco companies of intimidation tactics to silence critics
articles.description: Exclusive: Industry tactics are part of ‘deliberate strategy’ to distort evidence and weaken regulation, paper says Prof Charlotta Pisinger, a medical doctor and public health researcher, was speaking to this journalist about her experiences of intimidation by the tobacco industry when another complaint to her employer landed in her inbox. The Danish subsidiary of the tobacco company Philip Morris International (PMI) had just filed a complaint accusing her of breaching the University of Southern Denmark’s research communication standards for media interviews she gave questioning the safety of heated tobacco and vapes and whether PMI really cared about improving health. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
articles.description: The more you gaze at ​these 10 surviving works, ​with their cryptic inscriptions and even fool’s gold, the more the Flemish master trips you up​ – but being laughed at like this is all part of the glorious pleasure Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world. At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in

articles.title: ‘No publicist or manager in sight’: 80s Madonna, unseen and off-duty – in pictures
articles.description: In Madonna Into the Groove: An Intimate Portrait of the Queen of Pop , photographer Ken Regan opens his archive from 1985 to show never-before-seen photographs of the musician. The 160-page hardback showcases Madonna at her most vibrant, captured on a February day in Los Angeles, with accompanying biographical text by journalist Tomás Mier. With the majority of images previously unpublished, the book is a behind-the-scenes look at an artist coming into the peak of her powers Continue reading...

articles.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
articles.description: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suz

articles.title: ‘Perhaps we are safer not knowing’: a year after his death, Rob Reiner’s JFK assassination book is revealed
articles.description: The late director worked with David Hoffman and Dick Russell on a book about his lifelong fascination with what really happened on 22 November 1963 On 8 December last year, the great director Rob Reiner signed off the prologue for Who Killed JFK? , his book written with David Hoffman and Dick Russell and based on his podcast with Soledad O’Brien. Describing a lifelong fascination with the assassination of John F Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and what he saw as the vast conspiracy to cover up who really killed the 35th president, Reiner wrote: “Maybe, people don’t truly want an answer. Perhaps we are safer not knowing … Well, I’m done being safe.” Six days later, Reiner and his wife, Michelle Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home. Charged with murder, their son Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty . Continue reading...

articles.title: Flexibility more important to jobseekers than pay, global survey finds
articles.description: A poll of more than 40,000 workers found that a better work-life balance was the main reason people consider leaving their jobs Work-life balance has become the leading reason why workers consider leaving their jobs, according to a new global workforce survey, as flexibility is valued more than a higher salary despite the cost of living crisis. A poll of more than 40,000 global workers found that the top reasons for seeking a new role were better balance between professional and private lives, more flexibility over working schedules or remote working opportunities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
articles.description: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI has finally arrived. The new instalment of the epic crime saga is said to have cost more than $1bn to make and is widely expected to break sales records : some predictions put total sales at 40m copies in its first three months. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6, Robert Pattinson and Nathan Fielder | The Close Up
articles.description: Pulling a sickie to play Grand Theft Auto 6? Why is there so much hype over Nathan Fielder’s latest documentary about Elizabeth Holmes ‘You Can See Everything’? Join Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko as they discuss their favourite culture stories of the week.  Continue reading...

articles.title: Nothing compares to her: Sinéad O’Connor’s 20 best songs – ranked!
articles.description: The Irish singer-songwriter would have turned 60 in early December. To mark the occasion, we revisit the best of a catalogue that’s far more than a certain Prince cover This suitably uncompromising opener to the lengthy Faith and Courage offers a collage of radio static, Indian-inspired beats, dub bassline and whispered vocals. More importantly, it’s fantastic: you might call it trip-hop were Sinéad O’Connor’s vocal not so intense as to negate any potential for relaxation on the part of the listener. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘We don’t produce Neets’: the London school recognised at World’s Best School awards
articles.description: Swiss Cottage school for children with complex needs is place where ‘every child feels they belong’, education secretary says For Maria, the hardest part of having a child with complex needs has been the grief: mourning the life she had imagined for her son, for her family – and coming to terms with how lonely the reality of parenting him can be. “There are wonderful days but there are very hard ones too,” she added, tears coursing down her face. Continue reading...

articles.title: Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand harassed victims with YouTube message
articles.description: Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’ The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault. After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations
articles.description: Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case Lucy Letby’s lawyer has said the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns. The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin. articles.title: Prosecutors allege British woman ‘trying to find someone who would kill her’ lured to US and murdered
articles.description: Sonia Exelby’s disappearance sparked an international search. The accused man, Dwain Hall, denies murdering her Prosecutors in Ocala, Florida , have been laying out an extraordinary criminal case against Dwain C Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver accused of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, of Portsmouth, England. Prosecutors allege that Hall lured Exelby to the US before killing her in October last year and burying her body in a shallow grave in Marion Oaks. Hall has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Continue reading...

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.description: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 told it risks being ‘ghost’ summit as all mentions of fossil fuels removed from draft text
articles.description: Draft agreement also fails to show how developing countries will receive financial help to deal with climate crisis Cop31 live – latest updates Every mention of fossil fuels has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night , threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”. The second draft of the key text , released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey , removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis. Continue reading...

articles.title: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’
articles.description: The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam ’s version? AwapBamBoogers No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards. The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Movie

articles.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
articles.description: Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases. According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK , fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
articles.description: A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another. This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to

articles.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
articles.description: For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months. The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes , is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester , rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed,

articles.title: Here’s how we can give Neets a fighting chance | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle the youth jobs crisis Why is Labour reinventing the wheel ( Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people, 16 November )? There is an easier and less discriminatory way – and that is through the mainstream education system. This would not dump these young people into a post-16 Neet silo. Further education (FE) colleges have been working in the area of young people’s training and further education for decades. Yet the sector has been continually undermined by successive governments allowing terrible salary discrimination against the FE sector and by the need to chase numbers (and cash) for A-level-type students. And why has the FE sector has not spoken up effectively for itself? Continue reading...

articles.title: Should people like Nathan Cofnas be given a platform to express their views? Letter
articles.description: Raxa Mehta on Oxford University allowing Cofnas to give a talk on DEI, in response to an article by Ebony Riddell Bamber As a person of Indian origin and a staunch supporter of Amnesty International and a person’s right to freedom of speech and thought, I am conflicted about my view on whether people like Nathan Cofnas should be allowed a platform or not ( Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students, 15 November ). A huge part of me wants the likes of Cofnas to be allowed to speak provided there is a fair challenge and a decent debate where their ideas are debunked smartly, articulately and intelligently based on science and facts. Continue reading...

articles.title: Another fine mess for the flag-botherers? | Letters
articles.description: Pam Stanier and Dr Chris Haughton on people who put up union flags and hang them upside down It is surely ironic that the individuals who put up union flags frequently hang them upside down, as in your photo ( ‘Visceral response’: flag campaigns inspire anti-racism organising across England, 16 November ). The broad white diagonal stripe should be at the top nearest the flagpole. Displaying the narrow stripe uppermost is widely considered a sign of distress. Which is what I feel when I see a street sullied by the flags, whether hung correctly or not. It is an aggressive display likely to lead to disunity, not what the “union” should mean at all. Pam Stanier Malvern, Worcestershire Continue reading...

articles.title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
articles.description: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them ( Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November )? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt? We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it? Continue reading...
