articles.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
articles.description: IMMA, Dublin From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.” Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold. The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of the

articles.title: James McAvoy’s random encounter triggers a delusional fantasy in Parasocial Activity
articles.description: Òran Mór, Glasgow In Briony Martha’s compelling play, a woman generates an alternative ending to her impromptu meeting with the Scottish superstar Knowing what to believe is getting harder. Technology has blurred the line between truth and lies. Certain facts, though, we can demonstrate. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. We can also take playwright Briony Martha at her word when she says she bumped into the actor in a nearby coffee shop. It is even true that McAvoy was in the audience of Martha’s Parasocial Activity towards the end of this summer’s run on the Edinburgh fringe: a performance that can only have had a heightened air of unreality. At Òran Mór, Glasgow , until 21 November. At Southwark Playhouse, London , 13-30 January. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jeff Buckley was a 90s indie darling. Now gen Z think he’s the ‘yearner final boss’
articles.description: With his unguarded lyricism and earnest delivery, the late singer-songwriter is having a moment among a generation that fetishizes unrequited desire Sydney Tripoli has collected Jeff Buckley memorabilia since 2019. She keeps her collection of T-shirts, posters, vinyl and other merch celebrating the late singer-songwriter in what she affectionately calls her “Buckley box”. The 27-year-old scours eBay and resale sites for these pieces; lately she’s noticed the prices “skyrocket”. “During the pandemic, it was impossible to find Jeff Buckley shirts. Now they’re everywhere on Depop,” said Tripoli, who works as an actor in Los Angeles. “Now [my collection] is worth thousands of dollars.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The best early UK Black Friday deals on the products we love, from heated airers to the perfect pillow
articles.description: We’ve cut through the noise to find genuinely good early Black Friday 2026 discounts on Filter-tested products across home, kitchen, fitness, beauty and more • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Retailers aren’t rolling out their Black Friday discounts from the kindness of their hearts. It’s business. But if you can resist the urge to impulse-buy anything with a red ticket, and instead focus your attention on genuinely discounted items that you genuinely want, then it’s a potentially big win for you, too. The whole shebang lasts a fortnight these days, but it’s not quite in full swing yet. At the time of writing, the actual Friday in question (27 November) is just over a week away, and many of the best deals haven’t landed yet. Plenty of brands have been at it for days, though, with John Lewis, Boots and, inevitably, Amazon launching their Black Friday sales when you could still smell fireworks in the air. Continue reading...

articles.title: How beaujolais conquered the snobs
articles.description: Beaujolais is enjoying something of a renaissance, with even much-maligned nouveau gaining ground thanks to the fashion for light, chilled, low-tannin reds “Oh, it’s beaujolais. Fantastic!” My earliest memory of beaujolais isn’t of drinking it, but of saying it, on stage, as Beverley in a school production of Mike Leigh’s Abigail’s Party . Leigh wrote the play a few years into the British craze for beaujolais nouveau, the just-made, casual quaffing wine – historically destined for local consumption in France – that’s released on the third Thursday of every November. Sold cheaply, it landed beaujolais with an image that belied its extraordinary variety and quality. It was, says The Encyclopedia of Wine , “a self-administered cataclysm” on beaujolais’ part. Nowadays, it’s common knowledge that there is more to beaujolais than beaujolais nouveau, from its most famous village crus, such as Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, to higher-altitude, lesser-known villages that, amid the climate crisis, are now coming into their own. Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, with mostly granite-based soils to the north (perfectly suited to the red gamay grape

articles.title: I’m engaged but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel? | Leading questions
articles.description: Telling him would risk a lot of harm, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. If you’re going to take that gamble, you’d better be sure why you’re doing it Read more Leading questions My partner and I are engaged after a whirlwind romance, and I was over the moon when he proposed. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings. Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, says top commander
articles.description: The UK is conducting offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, a top military commander has for the first time revealed.

articles.title: Thomas Markle fit to stand trial over child abuse images, US court rules
articles.description: Thomas Markle is fit to stand trial on charges of possessing child sexual abuse material, a US court has ruled.

articles.title: Anti-monarchy group hands over 'evidence' on Andrew as it calls for investigation
articles.description: An anti-monarchy campaign group says it has given police and the Crown Prosecution Service "evidence" on Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.

articles.title: Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit
articles.description: BepiColombo double probe will map planet’s surface and study its interior to shed light on its unusually large core After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world. The BepiColombo mission will become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit. Continue reading...

articles.title: Terror on Bondi Beach review – these astounding stories recreate every single second of horror
articles.description: From agonised parents trying to find their children, to the man who tackled a gunman – these gripping accounts of the 2025 Sydney attacks should never be forgotten Milo Riley-Smith’s documentary is a simple piece of diligent work. It begins by spending a short time gathering the backstories of its interviewees: how they or their parents came to Australia seeking a new life, finding it to be a welcoming place where, as one woman remembers, Jews “could have a fair go” because anyone could, whatever their ethnicity. These Jewish Australians then talk about how, after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, they began to feel less safe. They had seen a flaring of antisemitic violence, vandalism and rhetoric; they attended the annual Hanukah festivities at Sydney’s Bondi beach with some trepidation. After an extended account of the events of 14 December 2025, the documentary’s participants comment briefly on whether enough was done by the Australian authorities to protect them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn
articles.description: Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled. Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction. Continue reading...

articles.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
articles.description: Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton Manchester City v Fulham, Saturday 12.30pm (all times GMT)

articles.title: Households stockpiling 'emergency items' boosts retail sales
articles.description: Shoppers appear to be heeding government warnings to stock-up on essentials amid a surprise leap in retail sales.

articles.title: Man accused of killing British woman sent knife with her blood on to friend
articles.description: A man accused of murdering a British woman he met on a fetish website sent a knife with her blood on it to a friend, a US court has heard.

articles.title: Met Police can photograph people without consent in facial recognition pilot
articles.description: Police officers in London will be able to use their mobile phones to photograph and identify suspects without their consent as part of a new facial recognition pilot.

articles.title: ‘We will become cyborgs!’ Peter Gabriel on bonobo ape duets, building a Jurassic Park for plants – and why AI will make great music
articles.description: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song

articles.title: Experience: I discovered my dad was a killer on the run – and turned him in
articles.description: After a childhood marked by horrifying cruelty, the day finally came when I held my father’s life in the balance Growing up, I lived in fear of my father’s moods. If there was too much ice in his drink or the sofa cushions weren’t lined up, he’d fly into a rage. He’d call me names and smash my belongings. Once, he broke a dinner plate over Mom’s head. Still, she remained devoted to him. My parents managed apartments in the US, so we moved around a lot. I never got to make friends, so I assumed all fathers were the same. Continue reading...

articles.title: From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK | Klaus Brinkbäumer
articles.description: As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back Dear British friends, Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja . Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing. Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany Continue reading...

articles.title: The male footballers best associated with each shirt number – the readers’ edition
articles.description: Last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers . Our readers spotted notable absentees so came up with an alternative list, which does not start at No 1 or end at No 50 Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. Thankfully our readers have provided an alternative list. And, creative bunch that they are, they have begun with No 0 and ended with No 51 … *** Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
articles.description: Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities • Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh . The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap. Emily Continue reading...

articles.title: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
articles.description: UK statement comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China. But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today. This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state. It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink. During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his E

articles.title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff
articles.description: Exclusive: Investigation launched after details of grief and trauma uploaded, raising questions over extent of issue The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers. Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP. Continue reading...

articles.title: Senior Tories urge Badenoch to drop Brexit talk in major strategy shift, sources say
articles.description: Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years UK-EU summit live: latest news updates Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years. While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject. Continue reading...

articles.title: Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers
articles.description: Woman who waived anonymity says she hopes her case will mean other victims of abuse are more likely to come forward A woman who was drugged and raped by her husband and strangers he had invited to their family home has been praised for her bravery in exposing the crimes. The judge in the case and women’s rights advocates said Joanne Young’s courage had been a feature of the trial. Her decision to waive her anonymity and attend court has drawn comparisons to Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged and raped by her husband as well as dozens of strangers in France. Waiving her right to anonymity, Pelicot said shame “must change sides”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.description: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down Business live – latest updates Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies. Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. Continue reading...

articles.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
articles.description: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Business live – latest updates Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 live: ‘We didn’t come here to beg’, African ministers say as climate talks enter final day
articles.description: Disagreements between rich polluting countries and everyone else threaten to push UN summit beyond its official end In a huddle outside the African group’s media conference this morning, Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings , Ghana’s environment minister and chair of the African group of negotiators, has laid out her thoughts on the proposed global electrification target that is now sitting as one of the agreements in the draft text of the “cover decision”. She said if electrification is included in the text without a means for African countries to develop electricity “then what you’re doing is creating a mirage”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
articles.description: Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Continue reading...

articles.title: British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces
articles.description: Exclusive: Guards told their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor that has rejected union recognition The British Library has sparked outrage over plans to outsource its security workforce and hand over to a private company three of its public reading rooms, to be “repurposed” as business spaces for hire – despite having reportedly received millions of pounds from the public purse to refurbish those spaces. Almost 70 guards have been told that their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor, STM, on 1 December. Their union, the PCS, has in turn been informed that STM has rejected union recognition for those staff. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest
articles.description: Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter. But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel
articles.description: Michigan senator-elect also secured a meeting with JD Vance, who called him a ‘terrible evil’ in lead-up to election The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump are in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office. “I agree with the president – I can’t believe I’m saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as Egypt and Saudi Arabia and Pakistan,” the senator-elect said. Continue reading...

articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
articles.description: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. Continue reading...

articles.title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
articles.description: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action • Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun ). But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science. ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick This is climate breakdown:

articles.title: Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep
articles.description: As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help “I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.” Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships
articles.description: Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change . I have spoken to people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s, describing age gaps far greater than three years; often with people twice their age or more. It’s noticeable that social norms and taboos didn’t change hugely between the start of the 1960s and the end of the 80s; in most cases, their pare

articles.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
articles.description: In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash. Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent
articles.description: The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black. “The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.” Continue reading...

articles.title: How to get a bigger Black Friday bargain: cashback, price matches and gift cards
articles.description: From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets. It could be a great time to snap up the things on your Christmas list or buy household items you need yourself. And there are ways to maximise your savings on Black Friday – which this year falls on 27 November – by doubling up on discounts, or earning cashback on your purchases. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Match review – conciliatory look back at England’s ‘hand of God’ clash with Argentina
articles.description: Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century , that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous cheating; what could they do in the face of such authentic genius? Over and above football matters, it’s clear to see that there were bigger things at stake. Rather obviously, it happened only four years after the Falklands war, which thoroughly poisoned already tense relations between Britain and Argentina. The Match si

articles.title: Richard Avedon’s rarely seen portraits of Hollywood A-listers – in pictures
articles.description: After consulting on the production of the 1957 musical Funny Face, which was loosely based on his own life as a young photographer, Richard Avedon considered leaving photography behind to pursue film directing. Although he ultimately remained a photographer, his fascination with Hollywood and its ideals endured throughout his life. Richard Avedon: Hollywood, a new exhibition, brings together more than 120 of Avedon’s iconic and rarely seen photographs of major Hollywood figures, including actors, directors, writers and composers, capturing the allure and influence of the entertainment industry. The exhibition was curated by the Richard Avedon Foundation and is on view at Gagosian in Beverly Hills, California, through 19 December 2026 Continue reading...

articles.title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts
articles.description: Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way. I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed with for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me. Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers

articles.title: Why I take this posh salt scandal with a pinch of you know what | Thea Everett
articles.description: The revelation that German rock salt is used in Maldon’s Essex-made product is causing a stir – but, however you sprinkle it, it’s all just salt This week, a report by the Observer found that the king of flaky salt, Maldon, was using imported German rock salt in its Essex production plant. It has since followed that Cornish Sea Salt (another industry leader) is also importing European salt in its production. There has been a food media outcry, with a tone that has felt very “I’m not angry, I’m just disappointed”. According to the Observer report, “tonnes of mined rock salt are being poured into the production line” at Maldon. The scandal is that Maldon calls itself sea salt (made by evaporating seawater), but rock salt is mined from dried-up underground seabeds (that were once also seas). Salt companies combine one type of salt with another to ultimately produce … salt. As food manufacturing goes, I don’t find it the most shocking transgression. “ Posh salt ”, once marketed only to the upper classes in Harrods and Fortnums, has been gaining popularity over the last half century. In the early 00s, the major supermarkets started selling Maldon sea salt, and over the last 20 years, wi

articles.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
articles.description: In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections. And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And

articles.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
articles.description: The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low. Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start. Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity Continue reading...

articles.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
articles.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme Continue reading...

articles.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
articles.description: Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams. Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
articles.description: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Continue reading...

If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations. Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. articles.title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
articles.description: The Russian film-maker spent 40 days in a coma and suffered 92% lung damage during the pandemic. He describes how making new movie Minotaur helped his rehabilitation Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.” Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma . He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.” Continue reading...

articles.title: NFL legend John Madden’s unlikely, unfiltered brilliance: ‘Coach was indeed animated’
articles.description: With the release of a new David O Russell biopic about the coach turned commentator turned gaming icon, those who knew him best remember his singular career Wearing his Oakland Raiders uniform and helmet, and gripping an orange traffic cone like a lance, Ted Hendricks rode into the training session on a roan horse and stopped at the 50-yard line. Some American football coaches might have reacted to the stunt with fury. But John Madden was unfazed. “We needed some relief from the intense grind,” recalls Hendricks, 79, who had borrowed the horse from a nearby stable. “It was a spur of the moment idea, but put a smile on everyone’s face. All Coach said once I dismounted was, ‘All right guys, Ted’s here, let’s get started.’ But I know he got a kick out of it too – just from the look on his face and the comments he made later in interviews.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Slightest Touch to California Schemin’: the seven best films to watch on TV this week
articles.description: A heart-shredding documentary about the beautiful friendship between Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell, and James McAvoy tells the cracking true story of two Scottish rappers pretending to be American Emma Fogarty is 40 and lives with epidermolysis bullosa, a rare inherited disorder that makes her skin incredibly fragile, prone to tears and blisters. She’s also good mates with film star Colin Farrell. Rachel Fleit’s heart-shredding documentary follows their preparations for the 2024 Dublin marathon, which he plans to run before pushing her in a wheelchair for the final 4k. Fogarty’s resilience in the face of near-constant pain is inspirational but hard to watch, while Farrell reluctantly allows cameras into his private life, physically squirming at times as he opens up about his addictions, sons – one of whom also has a genetic condition – and his beautiful friendship with Fogarty. Thursday, HBO Max Continue reading...

articles.title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
articles.description: (CDR) Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion. Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling lat

articles.title: Take That: Dreamers review – 50-something boyband fail to relight the fire on nostalgia-drenched return
articles.description: (EMI) The pallid disco revivalism sounds like S Club 7 and the folksy stomp-clap like Mumford and Sons – yet a few standout moments prove they can still strike gold if they try Listening to Wonderkids, the string-laden opener of Take That’s new album, it seems the three remaining fiftysomething boybanders are feeling reflective. “Forgiving you, forgiving me / This vicious circle is now complete,” sings Gary Barlow. In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. Earlier this year, they even embarked on a revival of their blockbuster 2009 Circus tour. Unfortunately, all this reminiscing has left their 10th album feeling so steeped in nostalgia that any moments of greatness struggle for attention. Continue reading...

articles.title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
articles.description: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his

articles.title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’
articles.description: The American novelist on the wild side of Maurice Sendak, re-evaluating Gone With the Wind, and the magical comforts of Alice Hoffman My favourite book growing up I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me. The book that changed me as a teenager A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living. Continue reading...

articles.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
articles.description: Sadler’s Wells, London In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness ‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it? Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths . Continue reading...

articles.title: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step
articles.description: The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower? But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride , has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. Yet they still keep coming (IP is king) and before the inevitable Shrek legacy sequel hits cinemas next summer, Netflix is trying to conjure

articles.title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
articles.description: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends • The best eco-friendly baby products Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need. There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for secu

articles.title: Chia pudding, pickle and picky dog food: whose fridge is this?
articles.description: ‘Elbow noodles’ for a pet? Obsessed with labels, and jam-packed with condiments, it could only be author and chef Carla Lalli … Cheese I pretty much always have parm or grana padano, and pecorino, for pasta, Caesar salad or a dressing. I’ll have a parmesan rind in the mix, too, for when I’m cooking beans or grains. Then, there’s snacking cheese: sliced cheddar, Pepper Jack or muenster from the deli section for a quesadilla when Cosmo [Lalli’s son] gets home. I love mozzarella sticks for a protein snack, or sometimes when I’m alone, I’ll melt them on stir-fried rice with kimchi, or Korean rice cakes. I always have them in the summer when I go to the beach, too. Marge’s food This is my dog’s food. The usual recipe is a mix of ground minced turkey, minced beef, chicken liver, chicken gizzards, carrot, butternut squash, some frozen kale or spinach, elbow noodles and rice. I truly did not think I would ever be this person, but she’s so picky about her food … I wonder why! But I did get sick of buying food and her leaving half of it behind. Continue reading...

articles.description: Maple syrup brings woody, caramel flavours to this yummy baked custard tart I’ve been using maple syrup as a sweetener more and more, because it tastes great and can be an easy way to introduce an extra woody, caramel flavour to bakes and desserts. Its delicate flavour can sometimes get lost in heavier recipes, but in this custard tart it shines, instantly making it feel more warm and cosy. articles.title: In a flap: how the butterfly became a symbol of gen Z resilience – and anxiety
articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. articles.title: Garden composting may not be glamorous, but it brings rich rewards
articles.description: It’s hardly the most exciting aspect of gardening, but getting stuck in now will leave you reaping the benefits in the new year I am going to do the thing that put me off every gardening book I read for the first few years of teaching myself how to garden, and smugly lecture about the importance of soil. But I thought it would be less painful in late November, that languid hinterland between the crisp crunch of bright autumn and the mania of Christmas. If you’d rather, I could bang on about tool-cleaning? Thought not. I am currently evolving into my next method of composting and getting proper compost bays. When we moved in, we inherited a couple of tall plastic bins – or “Daleks” as my fellow columnist Claire Ratinon calls them. Considering I’ve paid very little attention to the compost for the past 15 months, aside from throwing all of our raw fruit and vegetable waste in there, along with leaves and some cardboard, they’ve coped admirably. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: It’s been a strange year for seasons – now our fungi are in disarray | Michael White
articles.description: Cranbrook, Kent: Some species are absent, some have appeared twice – this may be a hangover from the summer drought and ‘second spring’ As autumn intensifies, it is easy for surface-dwellers such as ourselves to forget that we have already seen the trees turn once this year – not from shortening days, but for want of water. Summer turned leaves and meadows brown, until heavy rain in September and a second “spring” painted green all signs of the drought here in Kent, and banished at a stroke our fleeting interest in it. Subterranean organisms, though, and those that span both worlds, have far longer memories. The boundary oak between the lower paddocks will now for ever have a narrow growth-ring within its girth, and fungi, to the human eye at least, have been sent into utter disarray. Continue reading...

articles.title: Belfast Flood Alleviation Scheme Sept 14-18
articles.description: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme Training Exercise A training exercise to install the temporary defences will take place between 14 – 18 September 2026. This year the locations are: Harbour Estate Sydenham (Greggs Quay to The O2 Belfast) Sydenham (Pottinger's Quay) Ravenhill As part of the exercise, the slip road from Ravenhill Road to the Albert Bridge will be closed overnight between 11pm and 6am on Wednesday 16 September. If required , the closure may also be in place on Thursday 17 September again overnight between 11pm and 6am. Diversion signage will be provided, directing city centre-bound traffic via Bridge End and Queen's Bridge. There may also be some short-term disruption and temporary footpath closures at other locations. Advisory signs will be provided where necessary, including along the towpath. The Department would like to thank the public in advance for their patience. Further details, including locations and programme, are available at: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme | Department for Infrastructure .

articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
articles.description: The historian Stephen Kotkin of Stanford’s Hoover Institution has penned an important new essay on the phenomenon of “junk history”: reductionist or plainly wrong interpretations of historical events that have little or no basis in empirical reality but are nevertheless “marshaled in policy debates as justification for action, up to launching wars.” The emblematic example, which has recently been used by advocates for the war with Iran, is the failure of British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to truly ensure “peace in our time” at Munich in 1938. As Kotkin once put it, “It turns out not everything is Munich. It turns out Munich wasn’t even Munich when you get down into the nitty-gritty details.” Another example of junk history is what many otherwise well-informed American observers think they know about Sweden’s conduct during World War II and the Cold War. Aaron MacLean summarized this view well during a recent discussion I had with him on the School of War podcast. “I just associate (Swedish foreign policy) with neutrality,” Maclean said, framing the approach as an “attempt at splendid isolation from the affairs of the continent.” This neutrality, he continued, brought “some

articles.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
articles.description: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). This decision comes down to issues that have little to do with the act itself, nor even really with trade between the United States and these countries. Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. The preferential trade agreement — originally signed into law in 2000 by President Bill Clinton and most recently renewed in September for two additional years — provides duty-free access for over 7,000 goods to the U.S. market for qualifying sub-Saharan countries. In exchange for this preferential access, AGOA requires countries to meet a set of vague requirements, including reducing barriers to American exporters, ensuring governance and human rights standards, and not posing a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interest

articles.title: Not All Bond Carry Is Created Equal
articles.description: Not All Bond Carry Is Created Equal Authored by Eva Sun-Wai via M&G Investments' Bond Vigilantes , The word 'carry' is frequently thrown around in fixed income, and you will have heard many uses of it this year in the fashion of 'carry is back' or 'fixed income finally offers income again.' It is a crucial part of an underlying bond's return profile, and it is absolutely 'back,' but the purpose of this blog is to distinguish the important difference between having carry and being protected by carry. Today's starting yields offer an attractive entry point, but if the underlying bond is sufficiently volatile, a relatively modest yield move can erase a year's income quickly . When you factor in carry alongside rolldown and adjust for volatility, however, the 'carry cushion' can look pretty compelling. So rather than looking at bond markets and trying to time the perfect entry point, or simply choosing which bond market yields the most, the more useful question is: 'how wrong can I afford to be?' articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
articles.description: Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style. Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “ gjak ” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

articles.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
articles.description: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. Continue reading...

articles.description: At a restaurant in Italy in 2022, every forkful of my meal made my eyes close and mouth water. For four years since, I have tried to recreate this dish. The pursuit has finally made me a proper vegetarian I’ve ostensibly been vegetarian for 13 years and, in that time, I’ve eaten a lot of meat. My mum used to leave out the last bit of lamb madras, with a wink, then loudly announce that she was going to bed. I have accidentally found myself in KFC at midnight, hood up, drunk, looking both ways and asking for a Bargain Bucket. My partner once came home early from a night out and caught me red-handed, in bed with McDonald’s Chicken Selects. Such incidents were infrequent moments of weakness and, after the fact, I was always racked with guilt. But for most of my vegetarian life, I had felt a certain emptiness; a gaping meat-shaped hole in my heart and stomach. Then I ate a bowl of pasta. It was 2022 and an Italian university friend, Mattia, invited me to Tuscany. articles.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
articles.description: As a female bodyguard protecting an A-list star, the Gossip Girl actor shines in Christmas movie a cut above the competition Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff. Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
articles.description: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors? Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the p

articles.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
articles.description: Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place. It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back. Continue reading...

articles.title: This year, the Greens have reshaped British politics. Now we need party systems to match that influence | Caroline Lucas
articles.description: Without Zack Polanski and Hannah Spencer, we might still be stuck with Keir Starmer. But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaul Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP In the aftermath of some difficult weeks for the Greens, one encouraging response has particularly stood out for me: the widespread agreement across progressive politics that the UK is better for having a strong Green party. One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t. From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. As we increasingly win more council seats, assembly members, mayors and MPs, we are able, at all levels of government, to help restore the natural world, tackle climate breakdown and challenge the economic framework of neoliberalism that has governed us for too long. Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP C

articles.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
articles.description: We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice. Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of Dem

articles.description: New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday ‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’ Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start. United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt.
