articles.title: Danish MPs approve Greenland security pact with US
articles.description: Danish foreign minister says deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding Europe live – latest updates The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a new Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory. The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system. Continue reading...

articles.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
articles.description: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions. Continue reading...

articles.description: Harrowing accounts of the Hanukah celebration attack in Sydney last December. Plus: Marci Pierre White and Gordon Ramsay reunite. articles.title: ‘We can rage’: Michael Sheen fires up the gripping medieval epic Owain & Henry
articles.description: Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff Sheen is in wondrous voice as Owain Glyndŵr, clashing with Henry IV, in Gary Owen’s stirring history play for Welsh National Theatre No one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage .” Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre . Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play. Continue reading...

articles.title: Walk, eat, sleep: 10 of the best hotels for ramblers in the UK and Ireland
articles.description: As the new Good Hotel Guide goes live online, the editors pick their favourite places to stay for hikers and strollers With stunning views over Borrowdale, Donna and Gary MacRae’s small country house hotel is in a walker’s wonderland, with routes for all abilities, from the challenge of a Wainwright to a stroll around the wooded grounds. Donna and Gary can supply a packed lunch, arrange for a mountain guide and share information on favourite walks. For Gary, that means a scenic, “easy-going stroll” from Dock Tarn to Watendlath National Trust village and tarn; for Donna, a hike to the top of Rigg Head Quarry, then on towards High Spy, along the river over Maiden Moor and Catbells. Drying facilities, drinks and canapes and a four-course dinner await the rovers’ return. Doubles from £ 200 B&B (2-night min) , dinner from £55pp, no pets, no under 15s, hazelbankhotel.co.uk Continue reading...

articles.title: Thursday news quiz: A hungry hippo, a distant Voyager and a new James Bond
articles.description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare? The Thursday quiz spent the weekend up in Inverness where it was unexpectedly blinded by winter sunshine and met an awful lot of European herring gulls, including one particular persistent young chick that was quite adamant passersby should be feeding it. It clearly could not read the signs. Anyway, now is your opportunity to show you can read the signs, or at least read 15 questions on topical news, general knowledge and popular culture. There are no prizes except potentially a warm feeling inside. A considerably warmer feeling than Inverness at this time of year, at any rate. Allons-y! Continue reading...

articles.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
articles.description: Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November • Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie , say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Personally, I prefer to cook a cockerel on Christmas Day, which naturally gives me the

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
articles.description: Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan , whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat. The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. Hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, abandoned parks and wastelands are all places in which you might find yourself close to a plum tree; its branches decorated with fruit, some the size of marbles, others lozenges or eggs, and their spectrum of colour ranging from deep purple to powdery light blue, red

articles.title: Country diary: A luminous morning of gig crews and green and gold foliage | Virginia Spiers
articles.description: Tamar Valley, Cornwall: In the autumn warmth, the river brings flotsam and Canada geese, while a group of vintage Austin car enthusiasts have a picnic By Cotehele quay, on the last of a sequence of calm sunlit days, thin plumes of mist rise from glistening mudbanks and reedbeds glow luminous in the morning sun. Gig crews drag their boats up the slipway, away from the ebbing water. Lime-loving old man’s beard on riverside bushes reminds us of the cargoes of limestone, once shipped with coal to these quays for burning in the monumental kilns. Upriver, the woodland path towards the river cliff chapel is strewn with dry leaves, and beech and sweet chestnut hang on to green and golden foliage. The National Trust’s valley garden remains in shade, apart from the fiery top of a swamp cypress , brilliant against the blue sky. Continue reading...

articles.description: Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”. As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024 . A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. articles.title: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return
articles.description: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature. Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. articles.title: Woman raped by strangers after being drugged by husband calls for consent law changes
articles.description: Four men convicted of sexual assault and rape of Joanne Young, whose husband advertised her on UK swinging websites • Spiked nightcaps and invitations to strangers: how Philip Young sexually abused his wife for 15 years A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday. Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told. Continue reading...

articles.title: The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people | Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.description: Milburn’s review doesn’t ask what kind of work young people will be going into: zero hours, minimum wage, mind-numbing. Do we have the guts to solve that? One big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government. Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself. These figures have not appeared in any of this week’s coverage, but to understand the review’s context and its chances of success they are vital. Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
articles.description: Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask Business live – latest updates Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company . From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees . Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
articles.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. articles.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – an intimate meditation on family and memory
articles.description: The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.” Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime. Continue reading...

articles.title: Flottiana album review – 10-cd collection celebrates a very, very great Dame
articles.description: Lott/Johnson (Hyperion) We lost a truly singular talent with the death of Dame Felicity Lott earlier this year. This box-set brings together some of the British soprano’s finest recordings When Dame Felicity Lott died in May this year, the world lost a truly singular talent. An effortlessly elegant soprano, Flott, as she was known, was as at home in German, and especially French, as she was in her native English. This 10-CD boxset from Hyperion brings together some of her finest recordings from a career that spanned half a century. It’s curated by Graham Johnson, who in 1976 recruited Lott for The Songmakers’ Almanac, the pioneering vocal ensemble whose mission was to explore neglected corners of the repertoire. First, the voice; an instrument that appears incapable of anything indecorous. It never spreads or strays from the note, maintaining a purity and brilliance even when hovering in the musical stratosphere. Then there’s the diction, crisp and clear, wedded to an intelligence that lays bare the inner meaning of a song without mannerisms or affectation. With Lott it was straight and to the point, every emotion subtly and honestly conveyed. Continue reading...

The deal, which U.S. President Donald Trump signed in September with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, was formally ratified in a Nov. 19 vote in the Danish parliament, with 109 lawmakers voting for and none against. With their vote, Danish lawmakers gave parliamentary consent to an agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States that amends a 1951 agreement on Greenland's defense, established under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). While the 1951 agreement already granted the United States sweeping military rights in Greenland, the new deal strengthens certain access rights and allows the United States to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island . articles.description: Continuing Jobless Claims Unexpectedly Jump As 'Low Hire, Low Fire, Low Inspire' Economy Rolls On Last week we called it the labor market's trilemma: claims at 57-year lows, sentiment near record lows and a hires rate stuck at 3.4% (Nov 12). In his latest US Daily note, titled "US Daily: Adding A Third Hike" ( available to pro subs ), Goldman economist David Mericle expects a second 25bp hike in December and a third in March 2027, with the first cut pushed out to December 2027. In intelligence parlance, the tactic has an enduring name: the "honey trap" - known in Chinese as the "beauty trap." "Oh, that happens all the time," Boam told The Epoch Times. "The government sends a very attractive person, male or female depending on the American [target], to engage in a relationship with that person. And it's so common, it has a name. You've been honey-trapped." More than three decades later, similar counterintelligence alarms have resurfaced in Silicon Valley following the Nov. 12 resignation of Nvidia co-founder

articles.title: NY Times Thinks It's Unfair To Criticize Their Reporting
articles.description: NY Times Thinks It's Unfair To Criticize Their Reporting There's been an avalanche of pushback and a real pile-on (much deserved) against the New York Times in the wake of its story published this week entitled: War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason . The NY Times report is being widely seen as seeking to manufacture a justification for potential future US attacks on Iran's water and electricity infrastructure , given it presents them as serving a military purpose - and not as vital civilian infrastructure simply for providing water to the nation. This episode has reminded readers of the notorious Judith Miller days - who in the early 2000's served as the NY Times' mouthpiece and clearing house of pro-war propaganda making the case for Bush-Cheney's invasion of Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein.  As it turns out, there was no WMD to be found in Iraq , and Hussein was never looking for "A-Bomb Parts". This is also the era of the 'Niger Yellow Cake' hoax . articles.title: Trump Says US Rare Earths Production Will Match China's Within 10 Months
articles.description: Trump Says US Rare Earths Production Will Match China's Within 10 Months Authored by Jill McLaughlin via The Epoch Times , The United States should have enough rare earth minerals within 10 months to supply its own critical materials needed for national security, energy, and industry , President Donald Trump said on Nov. 17. Reaching the milestone would allow the United States to loosen China's grip on the world's supply of materials and minerals, and ensure its own supply chain, although one expert called the timeframe "unrealistic." "We are making rare earths at a level that we've never made before. ...We're gonna catch them within 10 months, they say," Trump told reporters in Manila during the first day of a three-day trip to Asia. The president made the remarks to reporters during a photo session with Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. They were gathered for a QUAD (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue) leaders meeting on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) conference. articles.title: Palmer Luckey's Secret $1 Billion Seastead Isn't What You Think
articles.description: Palmer Luckey's Secret $1 Billion Seastead Isn't What You Think Anduril cofounder Palmer Luckey says he has spent the years since selling Oculus to Facebook developing a seastead called SLAB, with "a 1,000 year design life," built to be "cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries." Billionaire Palmer Luckey (Getty) In a post on X Tuesday night, Luckey listed the industries he has in mind: "metal processing, medical research/treatment, desalination, oil refining, chemical engineering, and more." He said he and "a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017," and that while the project "still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion." He did not say where SLAB would float, what has been built so far or which laws it is meant to escape. Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life. articles.title: Electoral College Under Threat
articles.description: Electoral College Under Threat Authored by Joseph Burns via City Journal , With the 2026 election in the books, attention turns to what emboldened Democrats from state capitals to Capitol Hill will do with their newfound power. The press appears focused on hot topics like AI and affordability policies. But another item that could be on Democrats' agenda - and has received almost no media attention - may have an even greater impact on the nation's future. For the better part of the last two decades, far-left activists have pushed the idea of abolishing the Electoral College, not through the obvious route of a constitutional amendment but instead through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) . The proposal attempts to undermine the Constitution by having states pledge their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how the states voted. The compact, however, would take effect only when enough states to represent a majority of the Electoral College agree to it. That's what makes the results of the 2026 election so important.
